exemplar.title: What strong work looks like
exemplar.intro: Here is a Supply Chief writing up a DIFFERENT event — a spring picnic — so you can see the moves, not the answers.

traits.sample: 212 ÷ 30 = 7 remainder 2. Seven vans fill up and 2 students are left standing, so I ordered 8 vans even though the last one is nearly empty.
traits.why: The quotient alone is not the answer to a real question. Naming what the leftover is — students, not a decimal — is the whole skill.

traits.trait: Writes the equivalent division before dividing
traits.sample: $31.20 ÷ $1.30 is hard to picture, so I multiplied both by 10 and divided 312 by 13 instead. Same quotient, easier numbers.
traits.why: Showing the rewrite proves the decimal point was moved on purpose in BOTH numbers, not shuffled in one.

traits.trait: Estimates before dividing by a fraction
traits.sample: Each streamer takes 2/5 of a metre, which is less than a metre, so I knew I would get more streamers than metres before I calculated anything.
traits.why: An estimate first is what catches the 'multiplied instead of divided' mistake, which is the most common error in this whole project.

traits.sample: Someone could say 7 vans is enough because 7.07 rounds to 7. But rounding is for measurements, and 2 students are not a rounding error, so 8 stands.
traits.why: Naming the strongest argument against you and answering it is what separates a defended recommendation from an assertion.
